title: Explain the Union-Find / Disjoint Set data structure. How do find(x) with path compression and union(x,y) by rank achieve near-constant amortized time?
shortTitle: Explain Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union): find with path compression, union by rank
keyPoints: Union-Find maintains a partition of elements into disjoint sets, supporting find (which set?) and union (merge sets).
Each element points toward a representative root via a parent array; the root points to itself.
Path compression flattens the tree during find by pointing every visited node directly to the root.
Union by rank attaches the shorter tree under the taller one, keeping chains shallow.
Together, path compression and union by rank give inverse Ackermann amortised time, effectively O(1) per operation.
Union-Find powers Kruskal's MST, cycle detection, connected components, and fraud-ring clustering in banking.

s1_definition.oneliner: Union-Find tracks which group each element belongs to, and path compression plus union by rank make find and union almost O(1).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)** – a data structure that maintains a partition of elements into non-overlapping sets.
- **find(x)** – returns the representative root of the set containing x by following parent links to the element that points to itself.
- **union(x, y)** – merges the sets containing x and y by linking one root under the other.
- **Path compression** – during find, re-point every node on the path directly to the root, flattening the tree.
- **Union by rank** – attach the shorter tree under the taller one; only increment rank when two equal-rank trees merge.
- **Complexity** – amortised inverse Ackermann per operation, which is at most 4 for any practical input.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, fraud analysts group accounts into related-party clusters. Each account points to a head account, and the true head points to itself. To check whether two accounts are in the same cluster, Rajesh walks up to each account's head and compares. Path compression re-points everyone directly to the head once discovered, so repeated checks are almost instant.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Union-Find: Path Compression
  ═════════════════════════════

  Before find(4):           After find(4):

       0                         0
       │                       / | \
       1                      1  2  3
       │                              \
       2                               4
       │
       3                 All nodes point
       │                 directly to root 0
       4

  Union by Rank:
  ══════════════

  Tree A (rank 2)    Tree B (rank 1)
       0                  3
      / \                 |
     1   2                4

  union(A, B) → attach shorter (B) under taller (A):

         0
       / | \
      1  2  3
            |
            4
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Union-Find, or Disjoint Set Union, maintains a collection of disjoint sets and supports two operations: find returns a representative root identifying which set an element belongs to, and union merges the sets of two elements. The data structure is backed by a parent array where every element initially points to itself. Two elements are in the same set when they share the same root.

The power comes from two optimisations. Path compression flattens the tree during find by re-pointing every visited node directly to the root. Union by rank attaches the shorter tree under the taller one and only bumps the rank when two equal-height trees merge. Together they give inverse Ackermann amortised time, which is effectively constant for any practical input.

Union-Find powers Kruskal's MST, cycle detection, connected components, and dynamic connectivity queries. Its one limitation is that it is not easily decremental: you cannot efficiently split a set once merged, so it fits problems where sets only grow.

In the banking project at National Bank of India, Pankaj uses Union-Find to cluster accounts into fraud rings. When Rajesh discovers a shared device or phone number between accounts, he calls union. When Priya queries whether two accounts are in the same ring, the system calls find on both and compares roots, near-instantly even as rings grow large.

Remember one sentence: path compression plus union by rank give near-constant amortised time for disjoint set operations.
